utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon to everybody. Please, may I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please have 1D01231 up on the screens. It appears that this has not been entered into e-court yet, so I would appreciate it if the usher could provide the witness with a hard copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, apparently we do have the original in e-court, but not the translation, so I will read slowly, Mr. van Lynden. We see that this document is of 8th June, 1992, and let me just remind you that on the 1st of June, 1992, the cease-fire was signed, the one that was renewed and put in force on the 14th of June. The Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, strictly confidential, so this command is reporting to the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was called at the time. Item 1: "During the day, the enemy launched offensive actions from the city towards the suburbs. The artillery fire targeted Kobilja Glava Zuc, Boljakov Potok Zuc, and Han Zuc. He managed to capture the S-1 access from Rajlovac, Prijesko [phoen] Brdo, Smiljevici, Ugljesici [phoen]," and so on and so forth. And then it says: "The artillery fire targeted Vrace, Vojkovici, Nedjarici, Ilidza, Rajlovac, and the Military Post KAG. We're expecting a strong attack on the airport during the night." And then under number 3, it says: "A large number of houses have been destroyed in the area of Vrace. In the course of the day, we had 8 dead, 62 injured, 2 damaged tanks, and 5 transporters." Is this, in fact, similar or rather similar to the report provided by Sefer Halilovic to his Presidency on Serbian losses? This is of the 8th, and the other one was of the 18th. Do you agree that this is something that had to be actually noted, and the international public opinion had to be informed as to who was opening fire and who the victims were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a question, in light of what I experienced here yesterday. I'm not a lawyer, but as far as I'm aware, if the Prosecution has -- is going to tender a document, it has to shown those documents to the Defence beforehand. If the Defence is going to put forward a document, the Prosecution has to see it beforehand. But I have not seen any of these documents, and surely a witness has certain rights as well. How am I meant to react instantaneously to documents that I have never seen before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the Tribunal has the rule the witness has to be shown the documents he's going to see during the course of cross-examination. But you can answer as far as you can know. So if you have nothing to testify, you can say so. If you have any comment, you can make it in such a way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would like to go down that I think witnesses should also have rights to see certain documents. Mr. Karadzic requested to see me before the session in court, and I agreed to that. Mr. Karadzic could have been polite enough to show me those documents when I went to the prison to visit him. In response to your question, as far as I'm able to answer it, firstly, I was not aware at the time either of the documents you showed me yesterday and presented to the Court or of this report that you show to me this afternoon. If we are not informed, either by your government, and we had a producer and office at that time working in Pale, or if I was not informed on the other side of the front-lines by the Bosnian government, then obviously it is very difficult for me, as a journalist there, in what was still a fairly anarchic situation at the beginning of June 1992, to give that news. We gave that news as well as we could. We tried to check both with the Bosnian Presidency and with the UN then present in Sarajevo before sending our reports. As far as I'm aware, at the time our reports were as accurate as they could possibly be, given the limitations. And, of course, there are limitations to the accuracy of a reporter working in an anarchic war zone, specifically in a city like Sarajevo, being as dangerous as it was and as difficult as it was to get from A to B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, you see, this is not a document that I'm asking you about. It's really the events, and you reported on these events quite contrary to what is stated here. At one point, it was said that -- at no point was it said that there was an exchange of fire, that there were victims, and that the majority of victims were Serb, and you never reported any of that, because if one was to just listen to your reports, we would just hear that there was shooting in Sarajevo all over the place. And we can see here that there were dead and also a lot of damaged homes, and from your reporting one could not even divine that there were any Serb victims and that the Muslims were the ones who had actually started the fighting. So you're just pointing out these events because your reporting on them was quite opposite to what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, that may be in the guise of putting one's case, but it's really not -- it's really more argument without a question. Putting one's case, I would say, in general is saying what one's position is on a particular point that's in dispute between the parties, which Mr. Karadzic has done on the issues that this witness has to deal with. It's not continually, continually talking about injuries -- alleged injuries to your side, or things of that nature, and there was no question here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he was putting his case, and then the witness is capable of answering this question, in my opinion, as far as he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'll do my best, Your Honour. My first reaction is, as far as saying you expect me, on one side of the war zone, on one side of the front-lines, to hop over backwards and forwards to find out precisely what's happening on the other side. That is a ridiculous expectation of any war correspondent in any war zone. You are reporting from one side or the other. However, at that time, as I just mentioned, we had a team in Pale. We were in daily contact with them by telephone lines that still worked at that stage, and we asked them. At no time, Mr. Karadzic, did you inform that team staying at the Pension Olympic, with a producer who speaks your language, of any of these facts, nor did you offer to take him down there to see those facts. They asked. They were refused. When we, somewhat later than the events shown yesterday in this court, went to Pale and tried to film there from your side, we were arrested again and again. We could never work. Now, that's not my fault. That's your fault. If you were unable to put your case and give the facts, as you saw them, to an international audience, you can't blame us if we tried and were refused by you, your government, and your military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, one may interpret the accused's question to this effect: Watching your clip -- watching your video only, one cannot conclude as to the origin of the fire. What would be your comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My comment would be that most of the fire, not all of it -- we cannot vouch for all of it, and nor would I dare to do so, nor could we see all of it. I was at one side of the building, then at another side of the building. I couldn't see the whole of Sarajevo continually. Nor do I have eyes in the back of my head, Your Honour. Most of the fire we saw came down from the southern hills into Sarajevo, lying at the bottom of the valley. Therefore, we concluded that that fire came from the districts held, because the Bosnian Serbs held the southern hills overlooking Sarajevo, that it came from Serb lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me add one point. I'm not claiming that there was no return fire whatsoever, but nearly all the fire we saw and witnessed during those nights was onto Sarajevo. But there was also -- I mean, Mr. Karadzic mentions areas way to the west which were not -- we were not able to see. You can't be everywhere simultaneously. It's a large drawn-out city, Sarajevo, and that should be borne in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please do not begrudge what I've said. I'm really not trying to attack you. When we showed yesterday what Delic was reporting -- or, rather, Halilovic, on the successes against the Serbs, you believed that he may be overdoing it a bit, but from this document we see that he wasn't exaggerating. And I am just trying to show it to you, that the media did not report on this. So the international public opinion could have been misinformed. We did not start the fire. Their fire was the initial fire, and we just responded. Now, I would like to tender this document, pending its translation. Oh, it's been translated. We do have a translation, Your Honours, but it's not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have no clue what documents the witness and the Prosecutors have seen. Could it be brought to the Bench, the document? Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me. I didn't want to object, no objection to slow things down, but I thought if there were more documents that aren't in e-court, perhaps we it could use the ELMO, and then the documents could be broadcast since there is no need for these not to be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't say so because I was afraid it might be a confidential document. It seems to be an interpretation of the -- do you have the 65 ter number of the original, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1231. 1D, 1231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is not in the e-court. You said you have the original in the same number? No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again no objection. Could I just see the English translation. I saw it from a distance, I want to make sure I'm on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. They will be admitted, but MFI'd, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the question by Mr. Nicholls, the translations were sent by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have full translation, but it was not up-loaded, so that's why we didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's a draft translation, so it will be MFI'd, pending full translation. Sorry for the inconvenience. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be MFI D195.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 1D18 [as interpreted], please. I have the translation. These reports are in English alone because we did not have the originals, as we took this from -- it's 1218. This is not 1218, what we have before us. Could we please have 1D1218. Yes, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I will read this out in English, although we can see it on the screens: [In English] "Command of the 1st Romanija Brigade, strictly confidential, 11th of June, 1992. "Combat reports. Submit to Command of 4th Corps. "Enemy: "During the day of 11th of June, 1992, in the region of Vrbanja Bridge, PAM activities were spotted from the left side of the Parliament and right from the Vrbanja Bridge in the corner where the streets Gunduliceva and Branimira Cosica connect, also PAM and sniper activity was spotted. In the region where the streets Alekse Bojovica and Milorada Pejdalica connect, a bigger concentration of Green Berets was spotted, and it is assumed that their headquarters is there as well. At 13.30 hours, I got the information that from the region of the Zemaljski Muzej, there was an action from mortars on our units. And from the region of the executive council there was action with Zoljas and Osas on the position of the units 1st Brigade. Across the L oris a machine-gun nest was spotted, and behind the blue skyscrapers number 1, 2, and 3. Snipers were spotted between the streets Ivana Krndelja and Milutina Turaskovic --" I think it's "Djuraskovic." Also -- and so on and so on. Mr. van Lynden, you see the date here is the 11th of June, and they are swearing by cease-fires and truces, and yet you can see the fire that the Serb Army and Grbavica were under from the buildings that were south of Holiday Inn, between the Holiday Inn Hotel and Miljetska, the Zemaljski Museum, the government building, and the corners of various apartment buildings, the Parliament building, and so on. Was it really impossible for you to obtain this information and to report on it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, by the 11th of June I had left Sarajevo and was in Pale. Therefore, if I should have been aware of that situation, it is you and your government who should have made me aware of it. And we were not made aware of it, nor were requests to go to the front-lines honoured by you or your government or your military. My final point would be, in reading this, which I am reading for the first time, a line which comes up a couple of times talking about Green Berets. This is a figment of Serb imagination. I never saw units of people with green berets walking around in Sarajevo in June 1992. And those are the only comments that I can make about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. van Lynden, that is precisely the reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Morrison has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: You said yesterday, Mr. van Lynden, that you were aware of the Sarajevo-based forces having 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in June 1992. I saw them in March 1994. I never saw them -- personally saw them fired, but I saw them at a UN weapons collection point in March 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Right, that was my next question. You never personally saw them fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Because as an ex-mortar man, you probably would have taken particular notice of that, had you done so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware, but I didn't see it, that there must have been what I would call smaller mortar units, 60 or 80 or 120-millimetre mortars, that there must have been some on the Bosnian side. That's relatively close action, front-line weaponry. The 120-millimetre can be used to fire further. As I said, I never saw it being fired. I didn't see it being fired, either, on the Bosnian Serb side. The only time during the war in Yugoslavia I saw these units and filmed those units firing was outside Vukovar in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. van Lynden, that you should be able to see the two being fired so that you could report on who it was, who was firing? So did you actually have to see the weapon barrel? Did you see the barrels of Serb weaponry, or were you guessing on where they were coming from, based on the azimuth or some other data, whereas on the other hand the Muslim side would have to point out that the barrel was smoking, so that would determine who was opening fire?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see some of the fire coming from your positions specifically on the top of the mountain, to the position that General Mladic was to take me to in September 1992. Looking at the maps, we were aware at that time that that was an area controlled by your forces, and from there rockets were being fired onto Sarajevo. That, we could see clearly, and were filmed, and, indeed, a few of those shots were shown in some of the pieces shown to the Court yesterday. What we saw is you see where it lands, in which direction it's going. There is a trail. I mean, that was clearly visible in the images shown to this Court yesterday. What we witnessed in those early days of June 1992 was that most of the fire, not only, but most of the fire, the heavy concentration of fire, was incoming into the city of Sarajevo. As I said before, we could see that it was coming from the hillsides. There was trails of heavy machine-gun fire, probably anti-aircraft gun fire, and we could see the rockets. You could see these rockets. We filmed them, and they were coming from one direction, and they were landing in the city. And, therefore, from that we deduced where it was coming from and who was doing the firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Can we also know what is meant by Zoljas and Osas, in terms of the weaponry? Neither term is familiar to me. Mr. Karadzic, can you assist?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I can assist, these are hand held rocket-launchers. [In English] Rocket launchers from -- shoulder rocket-launchers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would be RPG-7s in the Western parlance, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yeah, I was in the army so long ago, we were still using muskets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the West, we never used RPG-7s. It's a Soviet-developed weaponry that was, I think, taken over by the Yugoslav arms industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Speaking of this, could we now please pull up P927 in e-court to take just a brief look at what this report is reporting on. And while we wait for it to come up, Mr. van Lynden, I am a bit confused that you see Hresa from the military hospital, which was impossible to see, and yet you could not see the area outside the military hospital from which fire was opened on Sarajevo. And, secondly, when you say on the 9th that rockets were landing on Sarajevo, do you exclude the possibility that Serbs had control over certain areas of Sarajevo; Nedzarici, Hrasno, Ilidza, Grbavica? So when you say that rockets were falling on Sarajevo, you should have pointed out which parts of Sarajevo, Serb parts or Muslim parts.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are again asking various different questions altogether, mixed up. I will try to take them point by point, beginning with the last point. I have just said that the rockets that we filmed landing on Sarajevo were landing on the main part of the city controlled by the Bosnian government. Those were not Muslim parts, as you referred to them. Serbs and Croats lived there as well. I did not see, and nor did we film, rockets land on the districts of Grbavica, Ilidza, Hrasno, and Nedzarici. You ask whether I exclude the possibility that Serbs controlled. I have never excluded the possibility. In fact, I've been taken, albeit somewhat later in September 1992, and again in February 1994, to those -- well, to some of those districts by your forces. I've never excluded that they were not -- were controlled by the Serbs. No, they weren't controlled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw your attention to this image. Could someone please switch on the e-court image for Mr. van Lynden. I believe he doesn't have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, I do. I think so. Is this the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like the witness to mark the image now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I would like to ask the witness to mark certain things there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, based on the report that we read out a few moments ago, where it said that fire was opened from the Parliament building, that's number 3 on your image; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see the Executive Council or, rather, the government building, and could you please mark it with number 6? That's the next number. The government building, the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, could we use the blue colour this time. Yes. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By June 1992, the only government building that I entered was the Presidency. These buildings -- I think the building you're referring to is -- I'll put an arrow next to it [marks], and this would be number 6, but I never entered that building. The Parliament building, as far as I'm aware, was basically a front-line position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've marked it properly. Yes, that is the government building, or the Executive Council at the time. It had been evacuated, and as you can see, it was used for combat operations. Can you mark the museum that is also referred to here, Zemaljski Muzej? That's the main museum there. It's referred to here as the location from where mortar fire came.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You state that the building was used for combat operations. I'm not aware of that. It may have been. I should like to point out to Your Honours that being based in building number 1, it would be very difficult to see fire emanating from those buildings going out, let us say, towards us from where this picture is taken. As to the precise location of the museum, to which, by the way, I never went - it wasn't a museum open to the public during that time - it would be somewhere towards where the photograph was taken from, somewhere in front of the Holiday Inn, somewhere in that -- let me -- very roughly in this sort of area [marks]. But from this perspective, I can't be precise. And, secondly, this is an area of town, Your Honours, that if you drove past it, you drove at incredible speed because you were open to fire. It's not an area where you ever stopped or walked around and checked the buildings, nor was I ever taken there by the Bosnian Army, so I cannot be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that it's perhaps a bit further to the left, underneath this arrow where it says "4." You can see a nice white building there, and then it's in that direction. But I think you're pretty close. Could you please put number 7 there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you remember where the street is that leads to Vrbanja? Well, maybe we don't even see it here. Where do you think that the Vrbanja Bridge is in relation to the Parliament building and the government building? It is the lower right-hand corner; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on this photograph, no bridge is visible, at least not to my eye at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the general area, the direction. Can you mark that for us? Do you know where the bridge was in relation to the picture we have here? Vrbanja, that's the bridge below the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that case, it would, indeed, be on the right-hand side of this -- of this image. So, I mean, in around here [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put number 8 there.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, you are at the military hospital. There's an exchange of fire here. All of these positions are to the south of Holiday Inn. On the other side of the river is Grbavica and Serb-held territory. My understanding is that if you are reporting, you should have reported about who was firing at who, or at least you could have said that it was an exchange of gun-fire and that you don't know who is firing at who. This way, your reports leave the impression that it's Serbs who are firing at the city and that they are firing from the hills. We'll go back to the hills now. What do you say to that? How come you did not notice that right in front of you, right in front of you literally, there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we showed the shooting. But as I have explained, from what we could see and what we could film, most -- by far the most was incoming into the area of Sarajevo held by the Bosnian government. As I mentioned yesterday, if there -- and this is in relation to my comments about the Marsal Tito Barracks after its evacuation, and this very precise artillery fire that descended upon that complex after its evacuation, that was a sign to us that your artillery observers had brought the fire down accurately and then there was sustained artillery fire for military purposes on that target. We imagined, although we did not go inside, the purpose was to destroy any military equipment that had been left behind by the Yugoslav Army after its evacuation, which would absolutely make it a legitimate military target. The fire that we observed in the rest of the city, however, was of a completely different nature. This was not sustained artillery fire on one particular point, which is what artillery is usually used for, followed up by a movement of infantry. Instead, what we got was fire all over the place, which made it extremely difficult to film, which is something Your Honours should bear in mind. You only saw a small amount of what was actually happening all over the city, and not on any specific point. We did not see that on the front-line that we have just drawn and that you've been referring to by the Parliament, by the Jewish cemetery, that there was sustained fire coming down right on that area, which would have been logical. You're right, it would have been logical. It's a military front-line. Instead, we saw it falling all over the place far away from the front-lines, and that's what we reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. van Lynden, that Sarajevo was full of legitimate targets, and also that the Muslim forces used trucks in order to open fire at our positions, and then they would leave that particular location? That's what a witness explained to us, that that was the customary thing, that a mortar is mounted on a truck during urban fighting and then it retreats. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that this happens. I have not seen, myself, a truck with a mortar mounted on it while I was in Sarajevo. However, I believe that under the Geneva Conventions, military forces need to be very much sure that if they return fire on civilian areas in a city, that they are actually targeting a military target. A truck that fires a couple of mortar bombs and drives away again, therefore, becomes a very hard military target. I understand that. I did not witness one of these trucks. I'm aware that they've existed, I've seen them in Beirut, but I did not see them in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to -- actually, this map has already been admitted, but could the notes be admitted, and also the map that we agreed upon with Mr. Harland. That's the relief map that the Prosecution has, and it is here in this binder that I received, and the number is -- well, of course, it has a different number now, since Mr. Harland marked it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you like to tender this map or picture marked by Mr. van Lynden now, or are you okay to delete this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I want it to be admitted, and also I want 1218 to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could kindly put your name and date on this picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D196, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it you do not objection to the admission of the 1D1218.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just wasn't clear. Maybe I missed something of the explanation of why there is no B/C/S original. Mr. Karadzic started to explain that, but I thought that it didn't appear on the transcript that I could see, or I missed it. But I'm just not clear on why we don't have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we got the exhibits from the Galic case, but we have these only in English. That's what it's all about. We could not obtain the originals. This is what we got from the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you like to mark it for identification until we get the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, I think if it was admitted in Galic, then there would be an original. We haven't -- Mr. Reid hasn't found it yet, but we'll see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you tell us if you find the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D197, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please have this map now, but the variant that we agreed upon with Mr. Harland, 02 from this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until then, Mr. Harland [sic], may I ask you the following: The fire that comes from hills and that falls on the town of Sarajevo, your understanding is that it is Serbs firing at the city; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm expecting Harland's map. Sorry. You're Mr. van Lynden, but it's Harland's map. So, anyway, on the basis of your reporting, if there is fire at the city coming from the hills, it's the Serbs firing; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The firing that we saw coming from the hills to the east and from the hills to the south would have come from Serb positions, yes. That's the firing we referred to, we filmed. You could see the rockets coming from that one position, Mr. Karadzic. That was a position commanded -- used by your troops. It's the position, I believe, that Mr. Mladic took me to when he allowed me to interview him in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you have the exhibit number of this map 2 in this binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, is there actually was no agreement on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the original, the original one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The original, yeah, we can bring that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unmarked original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, since it hasn't been agreed upon completely yet, can we get the map where the hills were marked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we can dig out the map marked by Mr. Harland, separate from whether we can understand it or not. I don't remember the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The unmarked, Your Honour, is 11790. I found that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The one marked by Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm still checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness would be benefitted if he could have an original copy in his front. I'm ready to show mine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that exhibit was D134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's try.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try. There is one that's even better than this, but let's try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, this is an aerial image of the Sarajevo Valley. Can you find your way here? Can you show us, for example, where the military hospital is in relation to this map?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not precisely from this height. It would be a more reasonable question: Can I say where the airport is? Yes, I can. Shall I mark the airport, begin with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's all right. I suggest that you use the colour red for marking that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the colour red? I'll just try. No, it's green, I think. It's green. Okay. So shall I put a "1" on the airport? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military hospital, you would like me to, I mean obviously roughly, mark this as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. Can you mark Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where Nedzarici is, the Serb neighbourhood of Nedzarici? Let me help you. To the north of number 1 and to the west of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right, thank you. Do you see the area between number 4 and number 1, the airport settlement held by the Serbs as part of Dobrinja? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part of Dobrinja would be to the south. That's Dobrinja [marks], unless you're referring to this area [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Precisely, thank you. Now, can I ask you the following: Do you see the letter Z? It is a Z with a diacritic. Is that the hill Zuc?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes. I mean, up there, it's to the north of the city, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you place a number there, and could you tell us who held Zuc?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. As far as I'm aware, in June 1992 it was held by your forces and was taken by the Bosnian forces towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see the letter H to the east of number 7, and to the best of your knowledge is that the hill of Hum, with the repeater and everything else we saw in the reports? Is that Hum?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be. I never went to Hum, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it can be seen from all positions in Sarajevo; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were hills to the north of Sarajevo. Whether that was Hum, I can't say that now, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the repeater that can be seen from all points in Sarajevo? It was on top of Hum. Is that that hill?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. I know the building you are talking with the television relay station. Yes, that could be seen, yes. If that is Hum, then it would be roughly there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can put number 8 there and tell us who held Hum all the time.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. As far as I'm aware, it was held by the Bosnian forces. But I was never taken there, so I didn't see that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see the letter G up here, and do you agree that that would be Grdonj, the hill of Grdonj that is above this entire north-east side and the old city? Was that also held by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't know. I never went up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But would you accept that, if I were to tell you that that is Grdonj, Feature 901, and that it was held by the Muslims throughout?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't contest that. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see the letter J to the east? Is that the Jajce Barracks? You'd have to know that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should I have to know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a striking building and it's a military facility, and they had considerable weaponry there.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not taken to the building, nor saw the weaponry there. But as far as I'm aware, yes, there was a barracks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you mark it there, then? That would be number 9 by now, because you did not recognise Grdonj.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let us move to the southern hills. Do you see where the red and blue lines are? Do you know where Colina Kapa is?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Bistrik Kula is?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken -- is this the same Kula as where there was a prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. The prison was in Lukavica. These are hills on the southern slopes on the southern -- in the southern part of Sarajevo. Do you know where Debelo Brdo is?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the name, but I can't pronounce it -- say precisely. I'm aware what we used to call simply Mount Trebevic as the southern hills. That's what we would refer to. Every precise name -- and we may have been wrong with that, but I'm not aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're right, it is Mount Trebevic, if we're going to call it a mountain. But the peaks on Trebevic, as you call it, rightly so, I mean, there are several mountaintops that are held by the Muslims, and they are closer to town, and the altitude is between 700 and 900 metres above sea level. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they are to the north, not to the south. And in my testimony, I referred to hills to the south and to the east of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Grdonj, the Jajce Barracks, and these hills in Trebevic; are they to the east and south of town?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trebevic is basically to the south. Grdonj, which you pointed out, which I was not aware of, is to the north of town. Jajce is slightly, it would seem, to the east, but still at a relatively low level near the valley bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we have an entire series of mountaintops on the northern slopes of Trebevic; that is, to the south of town. And these summits are held by the Muslim side. They have guns, mortars, and other artillery pieces. Are you ruling that out?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Bosnian Army positions are you referring to on Trebevic? I'm not aware of those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You claim that the Muslims did not have anything on Trebevic, that all of that was Serb held; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, as one follows the red line, one sees that the hills rise up from there, and that was Serb-held territory, as far as I'm aware. I'm aware that the Bosnians held hills to the north of Sarajevo. I am not aware of any high positions held by the Bosnian Army on Mount Trebevic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. van Lynden. It's much easier for me now. I see now that perhaps it wasn't that you were partial, but you were simply uninformed. The disastrous effect upon us is the same, but at least I see it wasn't ill-intentioned. Now, I'm going to tell you, Mr. van Lynden, which mountaintops were held by the Muslims on Trebevic. Colina Kapa, 966 metres altitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you say you're going to tell the witness. Well, that isn't really very much use. You need to establish the position by evidence rather than simply telling. What you tell a witness is not evidence in the case, in the same way that the question you ask is not evidence in the case. It's the answer which is the evidence in the case. And the witness is here to provide answers, not to be told matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, I could be pleased. The witness said that on Trebevic, on the southern side, the hills were held by the Serbs and that the fire from these hills was Serb. That is not true. They held more hills than we did. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, stop making your speech. Just put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think that you were supposed to know, nevertheless, who held Trebevic because you were reporting? You were supposed to know who held which position exactly.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In no war zone do the forces give you precise locations of where their forces are stationed or precise front-lines. Your forces took me on Mount Trebevic, Mr. Karadzic. They showed me their positions along -- over the -- on the mountain overlooking Sarajevo. At no time was I informed by your forces, Look over there, that's where the Bosnian Army is; therefore, we are in danger here, or we are being shot at from these places on Mount Trebevic. We were never told that. We drove repeatedly to the Lukavica Barracks from Pale --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- along over Mount Trebevic. We saw the positions there. We were taken there later. We were never, ever told -- I was never told, at least, that there were Bosnian Army positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just mark one last thing for us? Where was it that Mladic took you? Could you mark it on this map, please, with the number 9 or 10, I believe.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 10, it would be. I'm not sure that the position is actually on this map. It is to the east of the city. It was clearly within your lines, and it was a mountaintop position and you saw the whole town. It must have been roughly, but this is a rough marking [marks], where I've now marked number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is probably where Hresa is, or thereabout. Could you please just put your initials there, and then I would like to tender this map. Please put down the date and your initials. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The image marked by the witness will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have 1219, 1219. It's an e-court document. And this map may be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it to come up, Mr. van Lynden, please tell us which hotel in Sarajevo was torched? Which hotel was it? Which hotel had been burned down and torched by the time you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't stay there, for the obvious reason that the hotel had -- I think there was a hotel called Bristol, but I can't be precisely sure. When we entered town, we had been told by the Sky News correspondent who had been there previously, Dan Damon, that there were no hotels to stay at. He had stayed, I believe, simply in a flat with people. We were told that a hotel had been burnt. I think it was called Bristol. I don't know. I -- I mean, it's 18 years ago, and I didn't actually go there because it had been burnt. So, I mean, there's no point visiting hotels that have already been burnt in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, after this document, we will show that that wasn't exactly how it was. But here now we have the document, Mr. van Lynden, and it says "Report of the 16th of June." Now, on the 14th of June, the cease-fire of 1st of June came into effect, and we see now what was happening on the 16th of June, combat report for the corps command: [In English] "The enemy snipers fired from directions of Assembly, Bristol -- Hotel Bristol, Pera Kosoric Square, and during the night anti-aircraft machine-gun fired from direction from Assembly, and it burned second floor -- two floors in building from the right side of Zagreb Street towards the Vrbanja Bridge. Our forces intervened urgently and managed to localise the fire." [Interpretation] So as you can see, on that night -- or, rather, on that day there was fire, and a building in Zagreb Street, Grbavica, was set on fire, and that was rather striking. Did you report on that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, by that stage I was no longer in Sarajevo. I was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, on page 11 of the transcript of yesterday, you said that you were in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put the question to you, and we can take a look. And you also told us, during the preparations, that you were there in the Kosevo Hospital and then in the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered Sarajevo right at the end of May. I do not know the precise date of my departure from Sarajevo. But what we had to do on a daily basis is ferry our tapes from Sarajevo to Ilidza, where the producer from Pale would come to collect them. We would then go back into the city, i.e., we were crossing lines on a daily basis, and he would take the tapes to Pale to have them edited and then transmit the pictures to London. At around the 8th -- 7th or 8th of June, maybe the 9th, it was no longer -- we drove to Ilidza, but it was no longer at that moment possible for our producer to reach us, and we therefore took the decision that we had to get our pictures to London, that we ourselves then drove from Ilidza, crossing the airport, via the Lukavica Barracks, driving up Mount Trebevic, and drove to Pale. We then stayed in Pale for a number of days. We were then withdrawn from Pale back to London. And I only came back to Sarajevo towards the end of June.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have not heard this so far. You didn't state that for your statement, nor did you mention it during our conversation in the prison. Now I would like to tender this document. It was obtained in a similar manner from the Galic case, but we only have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we treat it the same as the one we saw before?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, although Mr. Reid appears to have located the original from the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have the number for the original as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I may have misspoken. I can't say that it was an exhibit or had an exhibit number, but we have an original.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm sorry, I believe now it was D241 in the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll keep it for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now please have 1D01098, where there is something mentioned about hotels. Yes. We should have a translation of this document. You can remove the Serbian version. It is sufficient for me to have it. I will be reading out from the Serb version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, this is an official note from the National Security Service, dated April 20th, 1992, an official note. On April 20th, 1992, through operative process, we have found out certain information about hotels in the city of Sarajevo. "Green Berets --" of which you claimed that they were a figment of our imagination, well, "The Green Berets have taken over Hotels Europa and Stari Grad. They have asked the Hotel Europa director, Ilija Macanovic, to leave the hotel in 10 minutes together with all other employees of Serbian nationality, under the threat of armed force. According to unverified information, one of the main headquarters of the Green Berets is located at this hotel. "We have also learned that on the 19th of April, 1992, the Green Berets have taken over the Hotel Zagreb. They demanded Serbian employees to leave the hotel under the threat of armed force. Along with Serbs, Muslim employees have left the hotel, due to fear from potential attack on the hotel." Mr. van Lynden, not a single hotel was torched. They were all captured by armed forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Sarajevo in April 1992. I did not witness a hotel being taken over by armed force. The only hotel that I ever entered in Sarajevo, but I did not stay there, was the Intercon in the heart of town. I did not go to any other hotel -- I didn't stay in a hotel when I was in Sarajevo. I stayed in the military hospital. Apart from that, I stayed in the building used to house VIPs, as I explained yesterday. So I'm not aware of this, nor, should I just add, was I ever taken by Bosnian Army, for instance, for conversations or to meet a commander, to a hotel building. So, I don't know, nor do I -- I'm not aware that I ever reported on how the hotels of Sarajevo came to close or claim to be burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 16 of yesterday's transcript, you said that you didn't stay at hotels for specific reasons, and what I have to point out, with all due respect, I have to ask for precision, because if the transcript leaves the impression that the hotels were closed because of Serbs and that that was the reason why you couldn't stay at a hotel, that would cast a certain image of Sarajevo. But now we see that you have actually said something else, and here we have proof that that was not the case. The hotels were taken over, Serbs were expelled from them, and this happened a month before your arrival, and these hotels then remained in the hands of the Green Berets, which were not a figment of our imagination. They quite realistically, actually, killed some of us. That's how it should be; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told, before entering Sarajevo, that there were no hotels open in Sarajevo. The manner in which they had been closed, the manner in which they had been burnt, was not something that I was aware of. That, I pointed out yesterday. I do not know, as I was not in Sarajevo in April 1992, whether this document is correct or not. I imagine this is a document written by someone who, himself, is not in Sarajevo, but is in Ilidza. I do not know the source of information for the people -- the person who wrote this document. I cannot, therefore, say whether it is proof or not. Coming again to the Green Berets, I never met anyone in the Bosnian Army who described himself as Green Beret. I met people who later described themselves as being members of the Black Swans, members of various corps, of various Tigers, but Green Berets was not something I encountered. I am aware that in Pale and -- Bosnian Serb soldiers referred to their adversaries as Green Berets. But my point was that I didn't actually see units walking around with green berets or calling themselves the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you believe Rasim Delic and Sefer Halilovic when they report on the forces at their disposal, and among others they mention that they have green berets, and they mention the number of men, which does not necessarily mean that they had actual green caps or green berets on their heads, but that that was what they were called; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- neither Mr. Delic nor Mr. Halilovic ever mentioned Green Berets to me in conversations that I had with either of them. And I haven't seen those documents until the documents that you showed the Court and me yesterday. That was the first time I had seen that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that document was obtained by the Prosecution, and it was a document of an intelligence service. And, of course, they wouldn't disclose their source. But now I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We admit it. It will be D200, Exhibit D200.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have some more time before the break? If so, I would gladly continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, we'll have a break now for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we begin, I'm afraid, Mr. Harvey, I didn't give you the opportunity to introduce your new member to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought I had done so on a previous occasion. But if I neglected to do so, my apologies to you and to Mr. Eric Tully, who is our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please pull up 1220 in e-court. We will go through a few documents briefly just in order to get a full picture of what was happening there. This, too, is a document from the Galic case, I believe. You can see it before you, and I will read it out in English: [In English] "13th of July 1992, regular combat report submit to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command. "During the day, the enemy at some moments carried out reconnaissance over our forces with small groups, and it opened sniper fire from the regions of the Mechanical Engineering Faculty, Parliament - Hotel Bristol. We found out that a bigger concentration of enemy forces is positioned in the rooms of the Technical School in the basement at the Marsal Tito Barracks. Enemy transporters and tanks were sighted in the Velesici region, not far from the tunnel, and above the house of the police three transporters were positioned, along with two enemy Pinzgauers."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, this is a report where we do not see that they dominated with their fire, but they were very active. And we also see what weaponry they had at their disposal. Do you agree with that? Do you see, for instance, that there was a transporter and a tank in Velesici, and so on?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that in the document, enemy transporters, which I imagine means trucks, or possibly tank transporters - I don't know which - and tanks are mentioned. I cannot verify if this information is correct or not. I didn't see that. To the best of my awareness, I was in Sarajevo on the 13th of July, 1992, but I did not see this. As far as I'm aware, also, this is a document that comes from your own army. This is not a document from an outside -- like the UN force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. van Lynden, this document is strictly confidential, and it is a military secret. And we see that the command of a brigade is reporting to the corps command. It's a genuine document. It cannot be more genuine than this. It does not mention -- it mentions sniper fire and some other movements, so it is genuine. In other words, in order for the Serbs to be believed, they would have to have Christiane Amanpour there on the spot. Now I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I comment on the comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are inviting the comment from the witness. Stop making comment. Yes, briefly, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, documents -- the veracity of the documents would be -- have to be seen to by experts, and I'm not an expert. Therefore, I do not know if this document is or is not genuine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm not sure why there is only a partial translation being admitted. Mr. Reid's found a translation of the full document, which has paragraphs 2 and 3 in it, which are missing from this. Three states that the situation in the territory of the zone of responsibility is unchanged and the units successfully control their areas. Paragraph 5 says that the morale is good and the security situation is good, and there were no major changes. Paragraph 6 talks about no logistics; difficulties. Paragraph 2 talks about fire from the Romanija Corps towards the Bosnian side. So no objection to the document, but we should have the full document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But does it mean that you have the full document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the number, which is ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's another Galic Defence document. It's not an exhibit. We have an ERN number, is what we have. Mr. Reid's been able to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll mark for identification, until we have a full document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll provide the copy to my friends during the break, and I don't know whether they have edited the document smaller. I notice that this one - I can't see the top or bottom - but it doesn't appear to have an ERN number, which the translation I have does have, so I don't know quite what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless you have an objection to the suggestion of Mr. Nicholls, we'll admit the full interpretation as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not object, but we did not edit it. This is how this document was used in the Galic case. Probably for the sake of court economy, they used this reduced version and they only used points 1 and 4. But we have no objection to the whole document being admitted. Could we now see 1D1221.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1220 is exhibited. It will be exhibited as ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D201, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite possible that this document, too, was admitted in a short form, but again it wasn't edited by us, but rather in the Galic case. So on the 19th of July, at 1700 hours, and I will read out in English: [In English] "Regular combat report for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command. "1. During the day, the enemy intensified its sniper activities, especially from the following directions: Para Kosoric Square, Bristol, Electroprivreda Company, social -- School of Mechanical Engineering, tobacco factory, Assembly, and Vrbanja Bridge. Mortar fire over the area of defence of 2nd Infantry Brigade around Vrbanja Bridge and Grbavica II is intensified. Grouping of enemy forces is noticed in the areas from where snipers were firing. They fired with rifle grenades and from infantry weapons from direction of Sirokaca towards Bosut Barracks." [Interpretation] If someone edited this document, which is possible, because we only see number 1, we do not object to the whole document being admitted here. But the editing was done by the Galic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, can you see that -- can you see what it says here about the activities on the 17th of July, Mr. van Lynden? Were you aware of this happening, that the Muslim side was active, as active as it states here?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that there was firing from Bosnian Army positions throughout the war. Apart from after the cease-fire in March 1992 -- 1994, yes, they were firing. Am I precisely aware of these incidents? No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know of these numerous civilian locations, schools, factories, a state institution, the social security building, that they were being used as military installations and that fire was opened from those buildings on Serbian neighbourhoods and outskirts of town?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware, yes, that there was a -- I was not taken there, but that there was a likelihood of there being Bosnian Army positions within the School of Mechanical Engineering. I got the name right of the Hotel Bristol earlier. I wasn't aware, nor did I go into the Hotel Bristol, which had been burnt, as far as I'm aware. The Assembly, this must mean the parliamentary building. Is that -- we were aware that there were probably army -- Bosnian Army positions in there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification, until we have the full original document or the full interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because I think that's necessary for the context to see how, perhaps, also close the nexus is to the witness's knowledge. There's only a small portion here, and what's becoming clear is what's been done is to edit these documents down to only showing actions of the enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D202.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 65 ter 11557, please. This is an OTP number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it to come up, Mr. van Lynden, I'd like to just tell you that this is your report of December 5, 1992, and there you're reporting on Otes. This is what we have. We see the first line. It says a report by van Lynden, and in English it reads as follows: [In English] "Otes burns. Four days after the Serbs launch their offensive, Sarajevo western suburb falls into their hands." [Interpretation] You see that is what you reported; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document, please, and -- oh, it's already been admitted as an OTP document. Could we now see 01194, please, so that we can establish here together, Mr. van Lynden, what was really going on. So 1D01194, please, on the monitors, and then we will see what was really going on around Otes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing so, could we have the exhibit number of this 11557.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P937.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There should be a translation. Yes, we have both versions now before us. Let's keep them both there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this is your report of -- this document is dated the 1st of December, whereas your report was dated the 5th of December. Here it reads "Regular combat report" at 1800 hours by the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to the Main Staff of Republika Srpska Army. Item 1: "The enemy has continued with intense attacks on the broad region of Ilidza and Rajlovac in the afternoon hours. The enemy has attacked from the region of Igman and the village of Kovaci, with heavy artillery fire, and with infantry fire from the town of Otes directed at Ilidza. In the direction of Sokolje Distribution Centre, the enemy has carried out an unsuccessful infantry attack, with the support of enemy artillery, on the region of Rajlovac." Under 2, it reads: "The unit of the Ilidza Brigade retaliated against the enemy attack with a successful counter-attack, and conquered the access from Azici to Nedzarici, as well as the centre of Otes. "Throughout the morning, the battles continue," and our forces linked up, and so on and so forth. Now, Mr. van Lynden, can we now agree that this actually was a Serbian counter-offensive and a Muslim offensive?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my understanding of it at the time. We went to the UN, and our information was based on what we were told by the UN. I should add for the Court that I was not, myself, in Otes, but the information that we reported came from the UN. I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will get to that. I would like to tender this document now, please, and I would also like document 0195 up on the screens -- I apologise, 01195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, unless it is objected to, 1D1194 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now have 1D1195. Yes, we have that. On the 5th -- well, it's the same date like when you were reporting. Again, the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, on the 5th of December, 1992, to the Main Staff. Routine combat report. Number 1: "Enemy actions. Throughout the day, the enemy has carried out the following actions: At 800 hours, fired artillery at the following area: Orlic-Smiljevici-Mijatovic hill, using 50 grenades and a simultaneous infantry attack on the region of Skravnik." I think that the interpreters have this on the screen. And they are asking me to slow down, but I thought that they could read this translation that is on the screen. "Around 1100 hours attempted infantry attack on Hadzici. "At 1135 hours precisely from the region of Brijesce Hill, using 122-millimetre Howitzers, fired 30 grenades at the region of Vogosca and Ilidza. "At 1215 hours, resumed attack on Orlic using chemical warfare (poisons) and artillery. "From the region of Kovac, opened fire at Vojkovici, using mortar as well as infantry." Number 2: "The Ilidza Brigade, in co-operation with the Igman Brigade, successfully carries out duties --" or, rather, "operations in Otes." Now, a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you really miss this 50 shells from the area of Orlic, and 30 shells fired at Ilidza 11.35? Also, would that not have been a top news item if you were to say that they were engaging chemical warfare and using poison against us?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did we really miss this? No, we reported that there was fighting going on. We don't sit at the top of a building, counting shells going in one direction or another. It's an impossibility, Mr. Karadzic. We are not an international organisation. We are a TV crew with one reporter and a producer and a cameraman. We film what we can. We were in the center of the city during that day, until in the afternoon, we were driving towards a TV station, and the pictures were shown yesterday afternoon. We were aware there was firing in various parts of the city. From where we were, we could certainly not see if anything was landing on Vogosca, for instance, but there was certainly firing going on and -- there was firing going on. That's that point. The chemical weapons, this is the first time I've ever heard of chemical weapons being used, which again brings me to the question that I have posed earlier. If you knew this at the time, why did you not bring Western journalists to such points and prove -- give them the evidence of what was happening? We were never told. We were not taken there. When we asked, we were never given this information. This is the first time, Your Honours, that I've ever seen this or heard this even mentioned during the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While I admit that we were not skillful enough in the media war -- actually, we did not even get involved in that kind of war, but we were hopeful that somebody would report, as they would report about the Muslim side. However, as for the previous document, you say Otes is burning, four days after the Serbs launch their offensive. So, in a way, all of your reports, and the reports of many of your colleagues, do not leave any doubt in anyone's mind as to the Serbs being the ones to attack and that it's always their fault. Did you not inform about that because you were ill-intentioned or because your editor changed this? But, anyway, would you agree now that all of this caused harm to us?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the difficult circumstances of a war, we reported as best we could, as accurately as possible, and tried always to check our information specifically with the United Nations, an outside force. We realised that information given to us by the Bosnian government could be tainted, as could information given by your government. We did as best we could, under extremely difficult circumstances, in an extremely dangerous city. And that's the only comment I can make about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you. Can this document be admitted into evidence? And then I would like to call up the next document. Now, that would be a film. We are going to see how the Italians managed in the same situation that you were in and how they reported. Could the previous document be admitted now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D204.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the transcript for this film please be given to the witness and to others. This film speaks about the very same event, at the same time, and we have a transcript here. And we're going to hear it in Italian, and we will see there are subtitles in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you -- just a second. If you have the transcript, the Judges should have them as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you should have received them. I was hoping that you had received them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is no one interpreting from Italian into English, but we do have the transcript, which we can read out. However, it is not our interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can have it placed on the ELMO, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we can view two things at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can have my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have no doubt that Judge Lattanzi could understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Sarajevo is in shock because the fall of the Otes neighbourhood after four days of siege. It is in the hands of the Serbs. This morning, our television news crew who had been involved in the clashes were trying to enter the city. Our producer has been wounded, the organiser, Roberto Canavicco [phoen]. But we should have right now on telephone live broadcast our reporter. Can you hear me? "Yes, I'm here. "So, first of all, how is Canavicco? "Canavicco has been by a rifle, a machine gun in his left arm. The arm has been perforated, and the bullet has stopped in the dorsal part. It is still inside the wound. He has been provisionally treated by a Serb first aid team, and we are trying to carry him to let him reach Split, where he will be able to undergo an operation or -- anyway -- "But where are you right now? You are no longer in Sarajevo? "We are outside of the centre, outside the zone controlled by the Serbs. "Listen, Demondino [phoen], what is the situation that you found during these days in Sarajevo? "A really dramatic one. We were trying to reach Otes. We were leaving the Serb zone in order to reach Sarajevo, and we found ourselves in the middle of a real battle. At least about ten shots hit our two vehicles, a small coach and a car, which penetrated glass and the external structure. It was bad luck. Unfortunately, what has happened, that they have -- and wounded our Roberto Canavicco."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. van Lynden, that the Italian reporter is reporting about fierce fighting in this locality of Otes? We saw that it was the Muslims who started the offensive, and the Serbs responded by a counter-offensive.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the earlier document that you showed. I have seen no other proof that it was the Bosnians who did the original attack, nor does it say so in this report by the Italian correspondent. In all honesty, I don't know who began that particular engagement at Otes at the beginning of December 1992. There was heavy fighting there. We reported that as well, and we reported that it had fallen into the hands or under the control of the Bosnian Serb forces, which appears to be correct. They -- from what I understand, the Italian reporters were on your side of the front-lines and trying to reach Sarajevo. I don't know precisely where they were, and then seemed to be caught in the middle of a battle between the two sides when the producer was hit by a bullet in the arm, which could have been fired, as far as I can gather, from either side. But that's all I gather from this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in your report which we showed, what was stated was that Otes fell into Serb hands four days after the Serbs had launched an offensive, and that harmed us, and it's not true; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
