utterances.text: We reported on the basis of the information that we were given by the United Nations forces in Sarajevo at the time. That's the one independent source of information that we had to go on at that moment in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please be a bit more specific. Who was it that gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember precisely who that was, but we would go to the UN headquarters and to speak there with one of the spokesmen. But it may have been on that occasion that we spoke to a military officer, but I don't -- I can't recall. We were there for two months. To remember every single conversation and whom gave us that information 18 years later, I'm sorry, I don't know the precise detail. But I recall that we went to the UN, because we did so on a daily basis, to get briefed by them as to what their information was. The UN had a lot more people there. We were on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps would dare to send a false report to the Main Staff and to General Mladic? Do you think that an officer would dare do that kind of thing? And why would he, anyway? What would be his motive to report in a secret report, which is not for the newspapers, that it was them, not us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it is for the witness to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I absolutely cannot comment on the actions of a Serb commander. That's an impossibility for me. Can we -- is it possible to switch the screen back, and then I can see --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As soon as we get the UNPROFOR report -- well, that's certainly going to be in the UN report, the weekly or the monthly one or the daily one. Can this film be admitted, along with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D205. And I also have a correction to the transcript for 65 ter 11557. It was earlier announced that it would be P737 [sic], but, in fact, it will be Exhibit D206. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D01207, please. While we are waiting for that document, may I inform you that that that is Zlatko Lagumdzjia's unit, the 1st Motorised Brigade in Sarajevo. He's a well-known politician, the leader of the party that was the successor to the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. Truth to tell, he did not sign the document. Someone signed for him, on his behalf. But just have a look at this. Have a look at what the order is and what the assignment involved is. Do we have the document? Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, we can see Zlatko Lagumdzija here, but we can also see that it's somebody else's signature. Nevertheless, it is his unit. Can we have page 2 now. 31st of December, 1992. Now let us move on to where it says "Task." "Task. Occupy region to the right. Transit to the left, most by Electroprivreda. Attack to be carried out through the direction of 11 Blue, south side of the Grbavica Stadium, palm, shopping, and 'strojerad', four big skyscrapers, with the goal to crush the enemy on the given axes and to occupy important buildings." Now, on page 3: "Fire support. Artillery support will be given in depth of the enemy forces." Then further on page 4 -- or, rather, the next page in English: "Morale." And then the last bit in "Morale," morale is high and so on: "Taking into account that it would be impossible to occupy such a fortified settlement without destruction and burning of buildings, which at the same time represent strongholds, everything should be destroyed and torched so that the operation could be successfully executed. Because of their well-known arrogance, none of the captured should be trusted, and especially the ones who carry any kind of weapon." Mr. van Lynden, the order is to destroy and torch everything. And as for those who are taken prisoner, they should not be trusted, especially not those who have weapons. So they are going to take prisoner -- as prisoners those who do not have weapons. And what does that mean, "do not trust"? That means liquidate. What else? So are you aware of this manner of treatment by the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before, and I am not aware of it, and I cannot comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you accept that this is a Muslim document? These are documents of their army; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. How am I meant to know? I'm not an expert on these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, can you see page 2 of the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Well, it doesn't depend on me. In the Serbian language, it is number 2, "Task." The first paragraph, number 1, is information about us, and we are the enemy. So it says "Serb forces," enemy; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm noticing the typography or letters. It's quite different when we come to number 2. Can you explain why it is so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is why: Because they became more pronounced because they had been highlighted probably using a yellow highlighter. The font is the same. However, the contrast is different, and that can only be due to highlighting. However, the OTP obtained this. They got it from the Muslim army, seized it. It's not our document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a reporter from the spot, you should have noticed the destruction of Raca, Grbavica, other Serb neighbourhoods, and also you should have been aware of the street fighting for each and every building. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were clear signals in Sarajevo that build -- that streets had been fought to and that there were front-lines and that these were pockmarked. When I was taken to Grbavica by your forces in September 1992 and again in February 1994, of course there were signs there. In my personal opinion, I would say that the damage there was much more limited than it was on the other side of the front-lines, but that is a personal opinion. But that I was aware of fighting, yes. But this document, Mr. Karadzic, I cannot comment on a document of that sort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this one I think I would object to. The witness has not been able to comment on it, add to it. It's a -- as Your Honours noted, it's very strange the way the document appears. But, really, this is not the appropriate witness for this document to be put through. He should -- I understand your Court's recent -- the Court's recent guide-lines, but I think under those guide-lines this document falls outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we agree with you, Mr. Nicholls. The witness was not able to comment anything about this document, and at this moment we are not fully satisfied as to the foundation of this document. So we will not admit it. That does not necessarily mean that you can't tender it through another witness who can give evidence as to its foundation. Let's move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me just say something very briefly. When there is yellow highlighting on a text, and then if that text is photocopied, then the letters seem different. This is a document that we got from the EDS, from the OTP. Could I now have another document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 11874, Prosecution number 11874.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In all fairness, this is not your report, but it's a report by your colleague from Belgrade. He's reporting from Belgrade about what is going on in Sarajevo, and it is the "Independent." Now -- "After Sarajevo suffered the heaviest night of bombardment by Serb forces in the two-month Bosnian civil war, local television yesterday broadcast intercepted radio messages from a Serbian general encouraging his officers to bombard the city without mercy." [Interpretation] See, that is our objection. Many correspondents sat far away from where the action was, and then they were buying the stories told by the other side. Now, Mr. van Lynden, tell us -- this is this well-known intercept of Mladic's alleged order. And now I would like to have the 65 ter number 30824. We can have the transcript or we can listen. I think that the transcript would be faster. So then we are going to have both documents admitted together. This happened on the 30th of May; whereas on the 29th of May, you were already there by then, there is this conversation between Ratko Mladic and Potpara, and then between Ratko Mladic and Varos. I can inform you of the following: These are officers who are encircled in the Marsal Tito Barracks. The barracks is completely under siege by the Muslim forces at that point in time. Right. Potpara, line 5 -- is it line 5? Potpara: "It is calm at the moment, but there is frequent activity from 1700 hours until 2000 hours, and six shells fell. A cadet was slightly wounded, injured." That is what Potpara is reporting to Mladic. And then Mladic, a few lines down, says: "Is there an operation going on?" And Potpara says: "Not right now. It is quiet. "Mladic: Be very cautious. They want to provoke --" And then a few lines further down: "Ratko Mladic: Look, by attacks against us, they want to provoke operating or acting in town." I think that the English page should be moved on to page 2, the English version. Potpara says: "Yes, all right." And then Ratko Mladic says: "Let the people know about that." Now we can move on to the next page in both the Serbian and English versions. Potpara says: "Yes." And then Ratko Mladic says: "Be extremely cautious and restrained." And then some 10 lines further, Ratko Mladic says: "And, secondly, they are trying, by attacking the barracks and the units, they are trying to provoke our activities and our opening fire on the town." This is already his conversation with Baros. And then Baros says: "Yes." In English, it should be on the next page, and in Serbian as well. The next page, please. Both in the English and Serbian, please, let's have the next page. Ratko Mladic says: "So there you go. You should prepare, and do not allow what happened to Jusuf Djonlic happen to you and all that shame." Baros says: "Yes." And then Mladic says: "We left all our weaponry behind there, all the heavy weapons, and yet they attacked our columns. And as for you, they would massacre you. Don't you worry. You will all manage to pull out. You are holding out. There will not be any problem." And then Baros says: "Very well." And then further down, Mladic says: "Don't you get carried away. Don't have illusions. We left all the weapons back at the Jusuf Djonlic Barracks. We left it behind." "Yes, yes." Next page in English, please. Ratko Mladic says: "If they're ready to implement the plan, they already received the first portion of all the weapons that belong to these areas, these four municipalities." So he's informing that the Muslims had received what belonged to them. And then Potpara says: "Uh-huh, uh-huh, yes." And then Ratko Mladic goes on to say: "They should have evacuated the Viktor Bubanj Barracks as well peacefully before the Djonlic Barracks." And then Potpara is confirming and saying: "Yes." And then let's have the next pages, please, in English. Toward the bottom, the portion where Ratko Mladic says: "I, too, am of the same opinion." Potpara was saying that he didn't want to risk his men's lives. And Mladic then says: "Well, it is also my position. If they want peace, they have it. And I ordered last night, as soon as I arrived, there was this mass -- or large-scale attack both against the units and against you. There was all this firing, and I managed to set people at peace there and put everything under control to stop the fire. As for what they're producing now, they probably have some pantomime performers or people who can successfully imitate the voices of everyone's, your voice and my voice and everyone else's." And then Ratko Mladic says: "It seems like they're making a circus out of everything there, and they're deluding their people, and it is not true that I gave any such orders." And then again Ratko Mladic: "So let them deceive and delude their people. You are to pass on this information to every single soldier. Do not mess around under any circumstances. Do not risk your lives, because nobody has a life to spare. We will not shell the town unless they violate the agreement and unless they put you in danger. But you have to be very careful. Do not trust them one bit." So here is this intercept, Mr. van Lynden. Can we conclude, based on this intercept, that General Mladic ordered that the old town, the old part of town, be fired upon, as it was reported in the Western media?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the radio intercept, I didn't report on it. Marcus Tanner of "The Independent" did. This is the first time I see this document, and I can make no further comments on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can we see from this intercept that the night before there was a large-scale attack -- a major attack on the Marsal Tito Barracks and that even a cadet was injured? And you could have reported on that. This was on the 29th of May, when you were already there; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On entering Sarajevo, and again I do not recall the precise date, we, indeed, went to the former military hospital and filmed the cadet who was being taken care of, who had been wounded in the Marsal Tito Barracks. And that was in either my first or second report that I sent from Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have this transcript -- this intercept admitted into evidence, 30824? That's the OTP 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about "The Independent" press report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't really care about that. We're not interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection to the intercept. If it helps my friends, the story that Mr. van Lynden referred to about the interview of the soldier who was wounded in the barracks is 40264B, I believe, is the 65 ter number for that story, which I did not play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The intercept is admitted. Just a second. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the opinion to admit the intercept in a comprehensive and strict -- following this strict principle, so we rather defer the decision to admit any intercept to a later stage, until we set out our rule. So on that basis, we'll mark that intercept for identification, pending future decisions as to the intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be MFI D207.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say what our position is. It is the following: All the intercepts before the war broke out, where the Muslim authorities intercepted the conversations of Serb authorities, are questionable, although they may be of assistance. But it really proves how unfair and unlawful the Muslim authorities were, rather than proofing anything against us, which is quite different from the situation where war has broken out, where both sides are entitled to intercept the other side's conversations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your next number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01128. While we are waiting for that document to come up, let me tell you what it's about. It's on the 23rd of April, 1992, a little before your arrival, but this is still about the JNA. It is one of their reports on the events in Sarajevo. The Command of the 17th Partisan Brigade is reporting. The document reads "Military Secret for Internal Use," information sent to the command for files, and then the following paragraph: "The political and security situation in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Military District," which means in the area of responsibility of the 13th Corps and the 38th Division, "is getting worse, which is leading to a full-fledged escalation into wartime conflict in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Military installations are especially vulnerable, the military industry and depots, and other installations and check-points of commands and units. The organisers of those attacks are: the Republican Staff of Territorial Defence and the BH MUP, Ministry of the Interior. And it is being implemented by paramilitary formations of the SDA and HDZ." And then two paragraphs below, it says: "On the 17th and 18th of April of 1992, the Green Berets and the MUP special forces, the BH MUP special forces, launched an attack on the Pretis factory in Vogosca," which was a military factory, among others -- other things. And it says: "In the course of the night, from 3.00 to 5.00 a.m., when 5 attackers were killed, 20 wounded, and 9 taken prisoner, they managed to take seven trucks, too, with ammunition, steal 100 Golf vehicles used by Green Berets. Through a speedy intervention by JNA units, a large-scale disaster was prevented. "On the 18th and 19th of April, 1992, the Green Berets organised the capturing of the military industry Igman at Konjic, which was cut off," the phone lines were cut off as well, "in order to prevent military response."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know of -- were you aware of attacks of this type against the JNA, while it was still the legal armed force in that area?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1992, I was not in Bosnia, and I am not aware of the events documented in this document, which I have also not ever seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, when you were to go to an area from which you were to report, do you try to obtain information as to the developments there? I assume that you knew where you were going, that you knew what was going on. Did you try and get any information about the area where you were going to report from?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. One gets as much information as possible from those who are there at the time. And on arrival in Sarajevo, the first place I went to was the UN headquarters to get a briefing from them as to the situation at that time. But as to the information in this document before us now, I am not aware of that. I may have heard something about it when I was still in London, but, as I said, that I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you get some information from your colleagues, the local reporters, the people who were reporters for TV Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember visiting TV Sarajevo during my very first visit to Sarajevo. I did go there at other visits. We were careful with anything that came from the press of either side who were involved in the actual war. My background has also told me that if I haven't seen something myself, if I hear something from another reporter, I also have to deal with that carefully, unless it is a reporter I know very, very well and know his work. So to answer your question about TV Sarajevo, yes, we did go there later during 1992, we did speak to people there, but any information that we were given by them we handled with a great deal of care.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see the second page of this document, please. And, again, let me just say that this is the JNA reporting to their superiors on the events in Sarajevo and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The last paragraph: "In the building of TV Sarajevo, there is a lot of dissatisfaction among the journalists because of the constant presence of armed paramilitary units who are on the premises of the TV, and for that reason the reports are one-sided and biased because they are submitted under the threat of arms." And as we can see from other documents as well, which I will show, the Green Berets had taken up these premises even before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that these premises were under the control of the Green Berets, in other words, of paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first went to TV Sarajevo, there were guards, as there are at any television station in the world. I didn't see paramilitary units, as you described them, there on any visits that I went to TV Sarajevo. That may have happened beforehand, as is indicated in this document. I wasn't there, so I cannot verify that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Bench will confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, to interrupt, but I believe there's no translation. So, in any event, it would be marked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness was not able to comment on anything. And as such, we have some doubt as to the probative value of this document. As such, we will not admit it. Mr. Karadzic, this one, as well as the previous one, is a kind of example you are wasting your time. You can put it simply to the witness, instead of reading out everything. I'm noting the time, but given the logistical problem, I'm compelled to ask: How much longer do you have? I'm asking this question given the -- considering the relevance of your questions that are being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, this is our position: I believe we still have a session today and a session tomorrow, and I believe we will ask for Mr. van Lynden to be recalled one more time. But why am I saying this? I am trying to put this forward because Mr. van Lynden and all other Western media actually portrayed the situation in Sarajevo that was very harmful to us. The maps and the configuration of the terrain did not -- were not consistent. All these documents, including the documents from secret intelligence sources, actually show that this was biased informing, or at least not sufficiently informed reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's for you, how to present your case and how to conduct your cross-examination. But on my part, I don't see the point of putting things when -- that took place before the witness arrived in Sarajevo. So I think you can be more -- much more efficient in your conduct. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 1D01224.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for it to appear, Mr. van Lynden, let me ask you this: You interviewed General Juka Prazina, and you were in his headquarters, and you assessed, quite correctly, that this was a mere criminal. And now I would like to show you what the Ministry of Defence, the Muslim forces, the BH government forces, is reporting on the 1st of June, 1992, the time when you were already there, and how they are portraying Juka Prazina. Now, let's see paragraph 2, where it says: "In this period, too, I contacted the military police reserve unit, Stela, that was located in the sports hall at Alipasina Polje and was under the command of Juka Prazina." "The reserve military police," so this is not -- they are not saying paramilitary forces. A state agency under the command of a well-known criminal? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my time, firstly, when I interviewed and saw Jusuf Prazina, he never told me he was a general, nor, as I recall, did he say that he was -- it was a police unit. He and his men simply called themselves defenders of Sarajevo. As you, yourself, pointed out, and as I pointed out yesterday, in my report I made clear that this was a man with a criminal record. There is nothing further that I can say about this. And, again, this is a report that I've never seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a document from the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic's ministry.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if they don't show it to me, how am I meant to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph reads -- that's where it is being reported as follows: "I claim that the orders of the Territorial Defence Staff of BiH, regarding the entering and searching of flats, are still being breached. Young and inexperienced people are sent to do this, and there are cases where items which are not subject to confiscation were found and taken from the people, which contributes to the dissatisfaction among the citizens and honest people." And then on the next page, but here it's on the same page in English; in the B/C/S, it should be on the next page: "I claimed again with full responsibility that a not-insignificant number of shells that landed on this territory from the aggressor's positions, that is, from the Lukavica Road positions and the home from blind children from Nedzarici, and that a large number of apartments and buildings were hit and some people injured and killed because of these youngsters who opened fire and provoked the aggressors -- unprovoked, even when there was no need for that, since no harm could be done to their manpower or equipment from such a distance. This uncontrolled shooting from rifles had always provoked a response with shells," and so on. And then further down, it says: "One more example, the freshest one that I could give to you as a proof of this argument: Last night, around 2200 hours, Juka's guys installed a PAM on a confiscated Pinzgauer, and yesterday, in broad daylight, they opened fire towards Nedzarici while a large number of people were walking around in that settlement, men, women, and children. And then they repeated this again around 2200 hours, targeting the crew of the tanks on Mojmilo Hill, on which occasion a machine-gun opened fire from a transporter, and then seven or eight shells were launched from the Zavnobih Square on the Lukavica Road, on which occasion there was some material damage, and thousands of people had to seek shelter in their cellars." Does this now give you a full picture of events in Sarajevo in early June 1992, where Juka Prazina and his men, as this reporter gently describes them, where his men are causing harm to both sides?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would certainly not describe this as a full picture of events in Sarajevo. This is dealing with one particular area. Again, I was not aware of this, nor was I told of what was happening in that one particular area. I was in Sarajevo at that time. When I met Jusuf Prazina, I met a number of his men. I didn't meet any boys. But I can't say to their level of training. That was not something -- and I was never taken by them into actual positions where they were shooting. I did not ever witness that, so I cannot confirm or deny this statement. My comment may well be true, but I would not say that this was the full picture of Sarajevo, but just possibly one incident in one part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps this was a misinterpretation. I said: Does this complete your picture of Sarajevo if I showed you what their ministry says about their general? Although I believe you're right, he was not a general yet at this time. I would like to tender this ministry document now.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this does not complete my picture of Sarajevo, to answer your question. And I'm sure there are still many things that I would need to learn to complete my picture of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted. But I note that we don't have full translation, so we'll wait -- we'll mark it for identification until we have full translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D208.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just put one more question. Could we please have 1D00129 on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for it, Mr. van Lynden, let me tell you the following: This is an initiative to -- 1D01129. So an initiative and a proposal to promote Mr. Adnan Solakovic and to confer a rank upon him. This is on the 11th of September, 1992, while you were there. Have we -- do we have it before us? Yes, here we have it. So it says here: "I propose," midway, "that Prazina Edhem - Juka, a member of the Main Staff of the armed forces of the RBiH and commander of the special units of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, be promoted to the rank of general." And then on the next page it says his units in Sarajevo have grown into an imposing brigade. And then after that, Juka's visions of formations, it says the result of this is reflected also in the fact that Juka's visions of formations have got the honourable name and task of special units of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then next, under 3 -- in Serbian, it's page 3 because -- page 3 in Serbian: "Because of this patriotic display of war skills, Juka, as the only one of all the war leaders who has grown from the popular resistance, is hereby promoted by the Presidency of the RBiH for member of the Main Staff of the RBiH armed forces and commander of special units. From all this, we see that Juka Prazina personally contributed to the preparation, organisation, managing, and commanding of units of the armed forces." And then signed by Adnan Solakovic. And then, pursuant to this proposal, he was -- he was promoted to the rank of general. Does this tell you anything about who our enemy was, Mr. van Lynden, who was on the other side?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I firstly point out that the date at the top of this document in English does not match the date of the top of the document in Serbo-Croat. One document is marking "September," this one says it is "November." Pursuant to your first point, that I was there: I was, in September 1992, in Pale, not in Sarajevo. I am not aware of this document. I have not seen this document before. And as I have already stated, I was unaware that Jusuf Prazina was promoted to the rank of general. I was never told that. After the -- my visit in the summer of 1992 to Sarajevo, I never saw him again. I believe he left Sarajevo proper, and that he was finally found dead in Belgium, if I remember correctly, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. The translation has the wrong date. The correct date is in the Serbian version. That was on the 11th of September. Now, even before the 11th of September, Juka Prazina was a member of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was a member of the Main Staff, a criminal who killed civilians, threw them out of apartment building windows, seized their apartments, and who knows what else he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to object on the basis now of relevance. The marginal, almost zero, relevance of this document and this topic, I would say, has been exhausted. It is now reaching the point where it is much more cumulative and time-wasting than probative. The witness -- right from the beginning Mr. Van Lynden said that Juka Prazina was a criminal, and that that's how he reported it. And Mr. Karadzic now continues to talk and talk and show documents saying that Mr. Prazina is a criminal. It's not something contested by the witness. And the witness has made it unclear that he is unable to speak to these documents. And the last one, the last question, Does this tell you about our enemy -- who our enemy was? Is a pointless question for this witness. It does not rise out of the direct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, before you decide, Your Excellencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not talking about Juka Prazina here at all. Juka Prazina is a symptom [realtime transcript read in error "similar to me"]. I'm talking about the Presidency that appointed him to the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, knowing full well who he was. We are going to show a lot of documents that illustrate that they were aware of who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It is for you to bring that evidence, but it is not for the witness to prove -- to make a comment upon those documents. That's why we deem it -- have a doubt as to the relevance of the document. The Bench will confer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just tell the court reporter that I did not say that Juka Prazina was similar to me. I said that he was a symptom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say something, what the point is, before you tell us what your decision is, why we are doing all of this? May I? Is it all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is our view, Mr. Karadzic: While we do not agree with Mr. Nicholls' observation that your question should arise out of the direct -- I'm not sure whether you said that or not, but we are of the view that you exhausted the topic with the witness. So the Chamber tells you to move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am going to move on. However, I would just like to draw your attention to the following: I would like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to this, and all the other participants. I'm talking here about a state that is not a state, that asked us to be subjugated to a state and social-political system in which Juka Prazina was a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll have ample opportunity to make your submission. This is time for you to ask questions to the witness. Do not waste your time. I'm noting the time. We'll take a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to let the parties know that we have decided to sit from 8.30 tomorrow morning to have a bit more time, and I appreciate the understanding of the staff. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is also grateful, because we do need time, indeed. Thank you. Could I now have 1D01223. This is Rasim Delic's book, and the title is "At the Helm of the Army in War and in Peace." Thank you. Page 100, please, and 101. Actually, I think they're together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, do you know who held Igman from the beginning until the end? This part above Hrasnica, who held that area?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 100 in the book. So it is 100 and 101, so it's the next page. No, this is 200 and 201, and I asked for 100 and 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Up until then, can I give you a bit of information. We saw that during the stage it was the Territorial Defence, we heard what Sefer Halilovic said what was in the area of Sarajevo. By now, it has already become the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; it's no longer the Territorial Defence. And here on page 100, Mr. -- well, the late Rasim Delic now says there are 12 brigades in town. We are going to find that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think it's necessary to read out all the portions. Put the crux of the content you'd like to put to the witness, and put it, and hear him what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 100, there is information about 12 brigades in the city of Sarajevo. Did you know that? Yes, no, that will do. I'll read it out. It's from the middle here, the middle of the first paragraph on page 100. In this operation, he counted on the engagement of the three tactical groups, Visoko, Igman, and Drina, involving about 10.000 soldiers and 12 brigades from the city, itself, that would be engaged from the inside. Then there is the police, in addition to that, and the Croatian Brigade Herceg Stjepan, in addition to all of that. Do you accept that, that they had 12 brigades in the city of Sarajevo, itself?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I have seen the book of Rasim Delic. I didn't even know he had written the book, Your Honours. I don't know that. He writes that. I don't know that, nor do I know if this is a specific moment of time. I don't know what year we're talking about. Nor does it seem to say, yes, 10.000 men. I see here "12 brigades." I don't know what a brigade was within the Bosnian Army, how many men that entailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't exactly 5.000, but it was three to five battalions, let me tell you, consisting of 500 men respectively. So it goes up to about 2500, but never mind. If you don't know about it, let's move on. Do you know that from Igman, there was very heavy fire that fell on Sarajevo, primarily the Serb neighbourhoods? But perhaps some stray fire went into other areas as well. Anyway, do you know that artillery fire continued against Sarajevo from there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never personally witnessed artillery fire from Mount Igman onto Sarajevo. And from our position at the military hospital, in the periods that we were there, if there was fire from Mount Igman, it would have been practically impossible for us to film, because it's way out to the west from the position that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 101 back. I would just like to read a small passage so that you see how much fire was coming from Igman. So it's towards the bottom of the second page. For example, Jusuf Prazina fired from Igman during the course of one day only, about 300 projectiles, 130 millimetres. That's a cannon, isn't it - against enemy facilities that could be targeted with 82-millimetre mortars. Also, during two or three days only, several thousand 120-millimetre shells were fired from Igman, twice as many as could have been provided to other army units, and so on. So Rasim Delic is criticising the excessive use of artillery and mortar ammunition from Igman against Serb Sarajevo. How is it that the world public was not aware of that, with that many correspondents in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour, but obviously I can't read this. I wonder if there is a date or time-frame to help the witness -- what the witness was asked about. We don't know whether this has -- when this is being spoken of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but it's impossible to find out without translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I can help, the only thing I can see is the 24th of "Octobra," which I imagine is the 24th of October, is mentioned just ahead of those projectiles. But Mr. Karadzic can correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, and further down it says the 14th of December, so it was already the second half of the year; 1992, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So with that, can you answer the question, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. Let me just go back to it. I was not aware of Mr. Delic criticising the excessive use of artillery, because he did not tell us. I did not meet General Delic until the following year, or even further, and right at the beginning of 1994, so I am not aware of Bosnian Army commanders criticising the excessive use of artillery and mortar ammunition from Mount Igman against Serb Sarajevo. I don't -- I'm not aware of any of the other correspondents at that time in Sarajevo - I wasn't there at that time in October; I was there in December - of a statement from the Bosnian Army command criticising the artillery or the use of artillery from Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My point here is the 300 projectiles coming from Howitzers and several 120-millimetre shells, the point is not the fact that they regret excessive use of ammunition, but the fact that Serb lives are lost in the process. And my objection is: Why does the international public opinion not know about that, with all of you being there in Sarajevo? However, the fact remains that that was not known of, and this Tribunal does not know about it or has not known about it until now. So, anyway, let's move on. Page 104.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a second. Mr. Karadzic, you asked the question in relation to the criticism of Mr. Delic. We were not aware of the criticism of Mr. Delic. I answered your question. That's the question you asked. If you're asking a separate question, why did we not report that? We reported that there was fire going in both directions. I do not recall specifically these events of the 300 shells that you -- that Mr. Delic writes about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I said that thanks to that criticism from their own sources, we managed to get information again from their own sources. So we're going to leave this book aside now. Could this page be admitted into evidence? Actually, I wanted to ask you whether you knew that the Muslim army had constant relations with Iran and Pakistan, and did you report about that? Did you inform the international public about that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not report, because I was not aware of any co-operation between the Bosnian Army and Iran and Pakistan, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We provided information about that, but we were not being taken seriously. We are going to abandon the subject, because Mr. van Lynden doesn't know about this. 1D01180 is what I would like to have now. 1D01180. While we're waiting for that, let me inform you this is the 6th of December, 1992. So you should see how accurate these reports are of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. We haven't got a translation yet, so I'm going to read this out. There's a hard copy, if somebody wants one, but I can read it out. The 6th of December, 1992: "Throughout the day, from 2.00 until 1700 hours, the enemy fired from artillery pieces from Igman and Hrasnica against Ilidza, Hadzici, Vojkovici, Lukavica, the Slobodan Princip Seljo Barracks, and positions of the 1st and 2nd Sarajevo Brigade. Over 300 shells were fired, and a great deal of material damage was inflicted." And then the last paragraph, number 7: "Two fighters were killed and nine wounded, two of them seriously. At Ilidza, 15 women and children were wounded." Again, there's a reference to 300 shells, just like the Muslim commander, Delic. However, this man is reporting about losses too. Fifteen women and children, Serb women and children, at Ilidza, do they merit the attention of international media? On the 5th, you reported about Otes, and this is on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They are worthy of the attention of the international public; right? Nevertheless, this was not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I do not remember being informed of that. I was in the Bosnian Army-controlled part of Sarajevo at that time, and it was no longer -- I would no longer have been able to cross over to Ilidza, as I had in June 1992. By that time, that would have been much more complicated. But nor do I remember being informed by this either from London, where the information would have been sent, I imagine, by your government, or finding this out -- this information in Sarajevo. It happened on the other side of the front-lines. While we were on one side of the front-lines, we report what we know of there. But certainly if I had been in Ilidza, yes, it absolutely would have merited reporting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would object, Your Honour. The witness hasn't been able to speak to it at all. The witness has made clear that he can't comment about it, that he was in the center of Sarajevo, that he wasn't informed about this incident, that he wasn't taken there, and that he couldn't have been there at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The same rule will apply. The witness was not in the position to comment on this document at all. On that basis, we do not admit this through this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I have 1D1222. Briefly, just one paragraph from this document, instructions as to how journalists should be treated, as well as UNPROFOR personnel. The 12th of September, 1992, that is the date. Page 3 of that document, item 18. Page 3, item 18, General Galic and Colonel Krsmanovic. General Galic: "Relation with members of UNPROFOR foreign journalists must be as correct and as civilised as can be and enable them to see our good sides and present it to our advantage."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that foreign correspondents had no interest at all in the Serb side of the story, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That you're talking utter nonsense. We went to Pale. We asked to work there. We went there in September 1992 and were, to a degree, capable of working. And in relation to the previous document, Mr. Karadzic, if you could stop talking to your colleague for a second, when we were there in September, we were taken to a front-line position outside Hadzici, a Serb-held position. It came under fire. We filmed it and we reported it. If you are taken there, we put it on air. If you're not taken there, if you're not given the opportunity to work, then you cannot report it. Furthermore, just on this general point, I would also point out to the Court that in April 1994, for reasons that the were never given, I was banned, indeed, for life by the Serb authorities, something that was also upheld when we asked by the Bosnian Serb authorities. Then it becomes impossible to report from your side of the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned arrests a few times. When were you arrested, when did you provide information about that, and when did you inform us of your arrest in Pale? Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't commented on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we do not admit it. The same rule, Mr. Karadzic. You didn't ask many questions about this, and then Mr. van Lynden didn't comment anything about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, these are instructions provided by the corps commander as to how journalists should be treated. This is directly linked to what Mr. van Lynden has been saying. He's been saying that we treated them poorly. It's the other way around. They treated us poorly, and that is why the response of our people on the ground was as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wasn't that the case? We were dissatisfied with international media first, and then we reacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber has given its ruling. Move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to have a document placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the first page, statement on Bosnia. So this conference pertained to all of Yugoslavia, but this particular document concerns Bosnia only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't that right? It's the end of August 1992. At that point in time, Vance and Owen took over from Carrington; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, could we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm just checking to make sure, but I believe this is in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, now we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I offer a document, just one sentence from it, which shows that Rasim Delic opposed demilitarisation in Sarajevo? Could we put it on the ELMO, please. And tomorrow we will show what General Rose had to say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honours, again it's an untranslated document that we weren't provided with before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you were notified of its use?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you give some explanation, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this is a document that was used by another Defence team, and it was admitted into evidence in that case. In view of the fact that the Prosecutor objects to the cumulative nature of the exhibits that we are offering for admittance into evidence, which we do not really agree with, we just want to show what was being reported in the international media, including the Sky News, and what the actual situation was in Sarajevo. And with this document, I'm just seeking to show that the other side, the opposite side, was against demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not raising that point. My point was simply the procedural rule we set up and you agreed upon. You need to notify the Prosecution in advance of when you start your cross-examination, of the documents you are going to use during the cross-examination; and you're also obliged to offer the translation. You didn't inform the parties, and in particular the Prosecution of this document, and even without translation. So what I want you to answer is why this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I've already said, we've given up and decided not to use many of the documents that we wanted to use because of the Prosecution's objection to their cumulative nature. And this is something that I wanted to clear up with this witness today, and that was mentioned in our interview. If you do not agree to this, I will withdraw the document, and I will ask for another one to be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you object to putting this document -- to using this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not on the basis of its late use. I just note that that makes problems for us, and that I hope it doesn't continue to occur, although I know sometimes things do come up. There's a pattern here. Mr. Reid has found a translation which we could provide to the Chamber. The relevance at this point is beyond me, but I don't object on the basis that it was provided to us late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was this: Mr. van Lynden, in our interview you said that you felt that our readiness and our agreement to demilitarisation was never taken [realtime transcript read in error "was taken"] seriously. In order to contest that, I showed the other document where I showed that we accepted, at the London Conference, to negotiate demilitarisation. And here in this document I'm -- In the transcript, it says that it was taken seriously, but your claim was that it wasn't taken seriously. And at the London Conference, we accepted that this be an item for negotiations, and from this document here, the highlighted portion, it says: "Demilitarisation of Sarajevo is out of the question for following reasons:" And then the reasons are listed. Can we now take a look at the bottom of the page and see that it was signed by Rasim Delic. Therefore, the question for you, Mr. van Lynden, is : Can we see clearly from this that it was the Muslim side who did not want Sarajevo to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I was just going to say, Your Honour, the only fair thing is to let the witness read the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but let the English translation be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'd ask that the witness be given a moment to review the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is quite a complicated document that I'm being asked to give an immediate reaction to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the question for you is whether it was the Muslim side who did not want Sarajevo to be demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document dates from April 1995, and not the August conference of 1992, so there's already a separation there. The document also is related to what is happening at that time in Bihac, in Northern Bosnia. So I don't see the link with your previous document of the August conference, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may -- well, we don't have General Rose's book in e-court yet. We'll have it by tomorrow. But the reports from 1992, 1993, and 1995, General Rose explains why the Muslim side refused the Serbian proposal for the demilitarisation of Sarajevo. But you've told us what you were able to. Can this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the face of the document, the Chamber is satisfied with the relevance -- its relevance and of the probative value of the document. Therefore, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D209.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 1D01141.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it to come up, let me just remind you. You said that you were in Hadzici. Was this in early September 1992; am I right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The later part of September 1992. This was outside of Hadzici, in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here we have a document describing what was happening to us on September 7, 1992, a report from the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps sent to the Main Staff. Under number 1, we see it says: "During the last reporting period, enemy actions became intensified through combined infantry and artillery attacks on nearly all defence lines. "We note: "An enemy infantry attack on Ozrenska Street was repelled, two conscripts lightly wounded." Did you know where Ozrenska Street was?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I ask this is that there was daily fighting there. Now, the next paragraph : "A strong infantry attack on Vojkovici area. The enemy attacked Krtelj and Krupac. And the first line of defence and the depth of our territory came under heavy artillery fire. Three conscripts were wounded, and one feature was damaged. "Heavy artillery fire against Ilinjaca," and so on and so forth. And then the next portion that refers to civilian. It says: "In Ilidza, there were strong enemy attacks and intense artillery fire on the centre of Ilidza. The post office building was hit, significant material damage, three soldiers wounded. The enemy shelled from Hadzici. No losses -- no personnel losses. Significant material damage." Then under number 3, it says: "The situation in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is complex, and shelling further exacerbates the difficult situation." Losses and casualties: 14 soldiers and 10 technical -- or pieces of equipment were damaged. So you can see that throughout September -- and you say that you were there in the second half of September, but here, this is a description of what was happening in the first part of September. So we see that there was fierce shelling of this part of Sarajevo. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there was fierce shelling of this part of Sarajevo at the beginning of September. I was actually in Pale. It wasn't mentioned to me, as I recall at the time, nor was I taken there to be shown, by either people from your government or from your army, that this was taking place. I was in Pale. We went into Grbavica. I never witnessed from -- while I was on your side of the front-lines, heavy shelling. I did witness that one shot was fired into Grbavica from the Bosnian government side, and that there was machine-gun fire in return. And we filmed that, and we put that out onto air. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, my colleagues told you about how to use your time for cross-examination or, in particular, how to cross-examine the witness. This question, to me, seems to be an example of a waste of time. You read out all the document, or most of it, to which the witness said, I don't know. You're reading out does not constitute evidence. The way you should proceed was to put your question, summarising the document in a simple manner, and if the witness says he doesn't know, you can bring another witness at a later stage, and then it is for the Chamber to assess overall credibility and what happened and what did not happen. So reading out the document is not a proper way of putting your questions. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were you on the 31st of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You weren't in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Sarajevo, no. I left Sarajevo before -- towards the end of December to go to Belgrade, because there were elections in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us then go back to something that you said earlier about the convoys in relation to Srebrenica. Could we see 1D00271, please. It says here that in your statement of this year, the 25th and 26th of February, 2010, on page 0674-9991, you said -- this is the same statement, several pages of it, and you said that you were in Srebrenica when you joined an UNPROFOR convoy, but that the convoy had -- the previous convoy was banned from getting through the blockade in Bratunac, where a fake protest took place. In other words, there was a fake protest going on. [In English] "For the benefit of the world media that was present --"

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I stop you here, Mr. Karadzic, because you're making a mistake. I was not in Srebrenica. I went with the UN convoy from Sarajevo into Serbia and then was with them as they tried to enter the enclave of Srebrenica. I wasn't in Srebrenica on my own beforehand. I went with the UNPROFOR convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But you said there that this protest was fake and that the -- that this was staged for the benefit of international -- of world media who were there, present there, which suggests that the Serb side wanted the world to be informed or to be told that this column -- this convoy was unable to get through. And what was the fake aspect, as you suggest here? What was -- how was that evidenced?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR and the UNHCR had had an agreement with your government that this convoy could, on a particular day, as I recall in November 1992, cross from Serbia, through the territory controlled by your forces, and enter the enclave of Srebrenica. When they tried to do so, they were stopped by the military and told that they would not be allowed to enter. We were then taken to a demonstration where the only banners of protest were in English; not in Serbo-Croat, but in English. The last time I saw that was in Iraq in 1980, when Iraq was governed by Saddam Hussein, and I and a number of international journalists went up to Iraqi Kurdistan and the only banners there were in English as well. That indicates to me that something was prepared for the world media rather than for the local people, most of whom -- in fact, we didn't encounter anyone who spoke English, when we actually asked them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then have 1D00271 -- oh, that's the same document, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, let's take a look now at this. I have a document showing that this was built into the document of the Main Staff. On the 28th of November, 1990 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... an unannounced column arrived carrying aid for the Bratunac inhabitants. There were six vehicles in the convoy. Now, do you -- would you accept, Mr. van Lynden, that a soldier is not allowed to allow through an unannounced column or convoy because he does not have the liberty to do that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, it wasn't a soldier. It was an officer. I cannot be certain of the rank, but as I recall, it was -- he held the rank of major. But it may have been a Potpukovnik lieutenant-colonel. As far as we had been informed both by UNPROFOR - and there was an UNPROFOR detachment with the column - and by UNHCR, which was responsible for the convoy of food, this was not only announced, but had been agreed by your government that on that particular date this convoy could enter the enclave of Srebrenica. Of course, it is possible that the officer concerned had not been informed by your government, and, therefore, because he had not been informed, he did not allow the convoy to pass. However, the convoy took several days before it was finally able to get into Srebrenica, and it can't have taken several days for someone to inform the officer that your government had given the agreement to the UNHCR and to UNPROFOR to allow that convoy of food to enter Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General Talic reported that this convoy was unannounced, and even had he been a general, unless he had approval from the state committee and unless this convoy was pre-announced, he would not have had -- he would not have been allowed to let them go through. And let's see what it says here, where it mentions the influence of the president, Mr. Karadzic: "The citizens of these places understood the situation, and after the convoy was checked, it was allowed through and arrived in Srebrenica on the same day." So it was on the same day, and not a few days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. van Lynden: Mr. Nicholls, do you have any --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. Just for a point of clarity, this is not a report from General Talic, the 1 KK commander. The translation I've got is that this is information which has been passed on to General Talic. And just the way the question was phrased made it sound as though General Talic was involved in this incident and was reporting what had happened. In my looking at this document, that is not correct. General Talic was head of the 1 KK in Banja Luka on the complete other side, so that's just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the end of the document, it says "Momir Talic, General," does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, but I think what General Talic is doing is passing on information he's received from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, Talic received from the Main Staff this information, and he's forwarding it further, but not in its entirety as received from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you remember the question, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I remember one part of it, whether it all happened on one day, and the answer is, no, it did not. We were there for several days, staying inside Serbia, before the convoy was finally able to pass. And as far as I'm aware, Your Honours, that was the first UNHCR convoy to be allowed into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what was your question, Mr. Karadzic, about the influence of President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, here the army reports that because of the influence of the Main Staff and the president of the Presidency, they exerted their influence on the people to allow this convoy to get through. And this was not the first convoy, but the nth convoy, but we will prove that easily. So here we have your allegation that this was actually a fake protest. And our position -- and we claim that it wasn't fake. And this document, strictly confidential, exchanged between commands of the Serbian Army reports that we had to use our influence to make the people agree to allow the convoy through. So that is my question. Why did you say that it was fake, when from this we can see that this protest was not fake?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already answered that question. It was our impression that this was an organised fake demonstration. And when the convoy was given the green light by your armed forces, we never saw any demonstrators at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may just say this briefly. You've said this a number of times, but now we hear you saying that this was your impression. So then I would ask you to always state clearly that it is your impression, and then we can easily work out the facts from impressions. So in the cases of Galic and Milosevic, these two received very high sentences, and yet they were based on impressions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of Mr. Milosevic being sentenced at all. Nor in the sentence of Mr. Galic, that was up to the Tribunal and not up to me, Mr. Karadzic. What we saw in Bratunac was a demonstration where the only banners that were held, or pieces of paper, were in English and in no other language. Therefore, we concluded that this was aimed at the international media and that this was an organised event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I was referring to General Milosevic, not to President Milosevic. Unfortunately, there are a lot of Milosevics here. But, Mr. van Lynden, what I am trying to say is this: Even if it was organised, it was organised by the people, because they knew that you were not reporting properly. And we can see from this confidential intelligence that they allowed the people to get -- the columns to get through. Can we have this document admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On that basis, and on the basis of relevance, we'll admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D210, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll rise for today. Yes. Judge Morrison has something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Just two things. First of all, just to clear one point up for me, please, if you could, Mr. van Lynden, in your statement you often talk about incendiary bullets or ammunition. By that, do you mean tracer rounds, or are you distinguishing between tracer and incendiary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean incendiary. A tracer round is different to an incendiary round, in my -- to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge, it is, too, and I was just wondering whether or not you made that distinction. It appears that you had. The second, really, is for you, Dr. Karadzic. Although it's not something you can be forced to do, by any means, but it just seems to me that with the relatively limited amount of time we have tomorrow, if there are any lengthy documents that you intend to put to Mr. van Lynden tomorrow, it might be a useful exercise to indicate which they are after we've risen and to supply copies. Mr. van Lynden won't thank me very much for extending his bedtime reading, but it might do some good for the efficiency of the court tomorrow morning. It's just a suggestion which you can accept or, of course, reject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So tomorrow we will resume --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, may I just reply? Since we have a lot of documents that are cumulative in nature, I, myself, was considering the possibility of offering them through a Bar table motion so that the entire documents could be admitted into evidence. And tomorrow I intend to show Mr. van Lynden numerous reports from other media, well-known media. Perhaps I could provide them for Mr. van Lynden to take a look at tonight, and also General Rose's book. And it is our view that something that Mr. van Lynden said here was rather vague, and I just want to be more precise about it. And I'm not saying that Mr. van Lynden did this intentionally, but, however, if any evidence is offered here and it is imprecise or based on impressions, then it needs to be made more precise and clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 8.30 tomorrow morning and go until 11.00, at which time Mr. van Lynden has to leave, during which session we'll have a 15 minutes' break. In the meantime, after the conclusion of Mr. Van Lynden's evidence, we'll have another 15 minutes' break and we'll continue to hear the witness, and we'll go until 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 21st day of May, 2010, at 8.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.06 p.m.,
